site.title: Think Before Sharing
site.description: Practical guides on Think Before Sharing, organized for fast browsing and comparison.

pages.title: Can You Trust What Found You Online?
pages.summary: Critical thinking in the age of social media and AI is no longer just the ability to spot a false headline. It is the habit of asking how a claim reached you, who benefits from your reaction, what evidence would change your mind, and whether a machine-generated answer is being treated as a shortcut for judgement.

pages.title: Accuracy Nudge
pages.summary: Small prompts to think about accuracy can help people pause before amplifying a claim that feels urgent or identity-confirming.

pages.title: Evidence
pages.summary: Across many experiments, accuracy prompts modestly improved the quality of intended news sharing, mainly by reducing false-headline sharing.

pages.title: Backfire Risk
pages.summary: Designs that make news posts more noticeable can raise engagement without improving truth discernment, especially when attention is not aimed at verification.

pages.title: Notes Timing
pages.summary: Community Notes can reduce the spread of misleading posts after context appears, but delayed notes show why pre-share nudges still matter.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Accuracy Nudge.

pages.title: Best Timing
pages.summary: Accuracy prompts are most useful when they appear just before a user shares, quote-posts, forwards, or otherwise expands a claim's reach.

pages.title: Sharing Gap
pages.summary: People often value accuracy but still share false headlines when social rewards, urgency, or group identity take over at the sharing moment.

pages.title: Nudge Design
pages.summary: A good nudge is short, neutral, timely, and targeted enough that it adds useful friction without becoming another banner to dismiss.

pages.title: Hallucinations
pages.summary: AI systems can produce confident, polished answers that include errors, fabricated context, or sources that do not support the claim.

pages.title: Fake References
pages.summary: Fabricated references can pollute scholarly writing, misallocate credit, and make evidence trails harder to trust.

pages.title: Bad Citations
pages.summary: AI citations can be fake, mismatched, or real links that do not support the sentence they appear to prove.

pages.title: Search Summaries
pages.summary: Search summaries can misread jokes, thin pages, or outdated snippets and convert them into confident public advice.

pages.title: Fluency Check
pages.summary: A smooth AI answer should be treated as a starting point until its key claims can be traced to reliable outside evidence.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Hallucinations.

pages.title: Legal Cases
pages.summary: Fake legal cases show how fluent authority can become costly when professionals skip source verification.

pages.title: Specialist Tools
pages.summary: Specialist AI systems can reduce some errors but still produce misleading answers when users mistake branding for reliability.

pages.title: AI Virality
pages.summary: AI-made misleading posts can be entertaining, scalable, and surprisingly viral even when they are not the most believable claims online.

pages.title: AI Detectors
pages.summary: As synthetic media improves, detection tools can become less reliable, making reader habits more important.

pages.title: Notes Data
pages.summary: Community Notes data shows what users flagged as misleading, but it cannot capture every AI-made falsehood on X.

pages.title: Funny Fakes
pages.summary: Funny AI-made posts can travel as jokes or visual surprises before readers decide whether they are true.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on AI Virality.

pages.title: Pope Puffer
pages.summary: The viral Pope puffer image shows how a playful fake can become a public test of visual verification.

pages.title: Small Accounts
pages.summary: AI tools let small accounts create highly shareable posts that can outrun follower-count expectations.

pages.title: Spread vs Belief
pages.summary: A post can shape attention and memory even when many sharers are not fully convinced it is true.

pages.title: Ranking
pages.summary: Critical thinking online starts with asking why a post reached you, not only whether the post itself is true.

pages.title: Claim Route
pages.summary: The same claim means something different when it arrives through search, a friend, an advert, a trend or a recommendation.

pages.title: Feed Controls
pages.summary: Buttons such as Not interested, hide, report and history controls can help, but their power varies by platform and feed surface.

pages.title: Feeds vs Search
pages.summary: Feeds often begin with a platform's prediction, not your question, which changes how a claim should be judged.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Ranking.

pages.title: Outrage Signals
pages.summary: Watching, pausing, commenting or sharing can teach a system that a topic matters, even when your real reaction is rejection.

pages.title: Similar Users
pages.summary: Recommendation systems can use patterns from people like you, making a narrow cluster of behaviour look like a wider reality.

pages.title: Viral Proof
pages.summary: A post can spread because it is useful, funny, shocking or divisive, so reach should never be treated as proof.

pages.title: Fake Authority
pages.summary: Fake council notices, invented quotes, and official-looking graphics exploit trust in institutions without providing real provenance.

pages.title: Safety Warnings
pages.summary: Police-like or council-like warnings should be checked through current official channels before they are shared in a crisis.

pages.title: Fake Notices
pages.summary: A council-style planning notice can look decisive, but the real test is whether the application exists in the public record.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Fake Authority.

pages.title: Correction Lag
pages.summary: False local notices can travel far before a council, police force or local journalist has time to correct them clearly.

pages.title: Quote Cards
pages.summary: A quote card is not proof that a councillor, police source or school official said what the post claims.

pages.title: Parking Scams
pages.summary: Fake penalty messages exploit the pressure of official enforcement, so payment links and appeal routes need checking before action.

pages.title: Screenshots
pages.summary: Screenshots strip claims from their source path, making reposted emails, notices and quote cards feel more official than they are.

pages.title: AI Tutors
pages.summary: Using AI like a search engine or tutor can be useful, but it changes how users should check accuracy and uncertainty.

pages.title: Citation Checks
pages.summary: A citation beside an AI answer may point to a real page while still failing to support the exact claim being made.

pages.title: False Confidence
pages.summary: Chatbots can produce wrong answers in a fluent tone because training can reward plausible guessing over honest uncertainty.

pages.title: Tutor Help
pages.summary: AI tutors work best when they guide practice, feedback and explanation instead of simply handing over answers.

pages.title: Grounded AI
pages.summary: Retrieval systems can reduce hallucinations, but they can still misread, overstate or omit important limits in the documents they use.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on AI Tutors.

pages.title: Source First
pages.summary: Some questions are safer to start with search results because the source trail matters more than a smooth explanation.

pages.title: Overreliance
pages.summary: A chatbot tutor can weaken learning when trust, convenience or quick answers replace struggle, recall and self-correction.

pages.title: Name Claim
pages.summary: Fact-checking becomes easier when the reader first states the exact claim instead of reacting to the whole post.

pages.title: AI Claims
pages.summary: Fluent AI text can sound organised while blending facts, invented details, and vague assertions that must be split apart.

pages.title: Search Wording
pages.summary: Search tools may miss a fact check until the claim is rephrased with clearer names, dates, and technical terms.

pages.title: Fact Checkers
pages.summary: Fact-checkers first define the exact assertion of public interest so evidence can be applied consistently and fairly.

pages.title: Photos Videos
pages.summary: Images and clips need claims about place, date, source, and context before reverse searches or archives can help.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Name Claim.

pages.title: False Causes
pages.summary: A number may be accurate while the post around it pushes readers toward a cause the evidence does not support.

pages.title: Vague Posts
pages.summary: A vague post becomes easier to test when the reader rewrites it as one precise question that evidence could answer.

pages.title: Community Notes
pages.summary: Crowd-sourced correction can add context to misleading posts, but readers still need to judge speed, coverage, and source quality.

pages.title: AI Scale
pages.summary: AI tools can create plausible false images and claims faster than human note systems can reliably review them.

pages.title: Bridging
pages.summary: Community Notes depend on agreement across contributors with different rating histories, not just a simple majority vote.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Community Notes.

pages.title: Late Notes
pages.summary: Community Notes can reduce sharing once visible, but the fastest spread often happens before contributors reach agreement.

pages.title: No Note
pages.summary: The absence of a public note may reflect delay, disagreement, low visibility or contributor limits rather than accuracy.

pages.title: Source Check
pages.summary: A helpful note is only as strong as the source trail it gives readers for checking the original claim.

pages.title: Fact Checks
pages.summary: Community Notes and professional fact-checkers often correct different posts, and the strongest public corrections may need both.

pages.title: Not Cynicism
pages.summary: Healthy scepticism asks for evidence and context, while cynicism treats everything as fake and can become another shortcut.

pages.title: Blanket distrust
pages.summary: Cynicism can feel protective online, but it often replaces evidence with emotional shortcuts and familiar voices.

pages.title: Corrections
pages.summary: Responsible updates can look suspicious to cynical readers, even when changing the record is part of getting closer to truth.

pages.title: Deepfake doubt
pages.summary: Fear of synthetic media can help people spot fakes, but it can also give bad actors a reason to deny authentic evidence.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Not Cynicism.

pages.title: Popularity cues
pages.summary: Likes, views and confident delivery can make weak claims look credible even when creators have not checked the facts.

pages.title: Repetition
pages.summary: Repeated claims can start to feel true, so cynical readers still need to check whether many posts share one real source.

pages.title: Trust calibration
pages.summary: Teaching people to distrust everything can backfire unless it also helps them separate stronger evidence from weaker claims.

pages.title: Deepfakes
pages.summary: Synthetic voices and videos require new habits for checking provenance, corroboration, and the original recording context.

pages.title: Biden Robocall
pages.summary: The New Hampshire robocall showed why investigators trace telecom routes and campaign links instead of relying on listeners' ears.

pages.title: Credentials
pages.summary: Provenance labels can show parts of a file's history, but they cannot prove every claim attached to the media.

pages.title: Detector Scores
pages.summary: Detector results can help triage suspicious media, but new generators, compression and unfamiliar formats can break confidence.

pages.title: First Upload
pages.summary: The first upload trail often tells more than the clip itself, especially when reposts strip context and reward speed.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Deepfakes.

pages.title: Video Fraud
pages.summary: A video meeting can feel socially real, but unusual financial requests still need independent approval channels.

pages.title: Voice Scams
pages.summary: A familiar voice is not enough proof when a caller creates panic, urgency or pressure to send money.

pages.title: Emotional Posts
pages.summary: Posts that provoke anger, fear, pride, or moral certainty deserve extra caution because emotional force is not evidence.

pages.title: AI polish
pages.summary: AI tools can make emotional misinformation look professional, local, and confident even when the underlying evidence is thin.

pages.title: Fear urgency
pages.summary: Fear posts can seem protective in a crisis, but urgent instructions often push weak claims ahead of reliable information.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Emotional Posts.

pages.title: Outrage
pages.summary: Outrage can turn sharing into a loyalty signal before readers have checked whether the claim is true or fair.

pages.title: Pride claims
pages.summary: Pride-based misinformation feels safer than outrage, but it can still make readers accept claims because they flatter a group identity.

pages.title: Social rewards
pages.summary: Likes and shares can teach users that more outraged posts get more attention, making emotional escalation feel normal.

pages.title: Moral pressure
pages.summary: Some posts make asking for evidence seem immoral, which is why scepticism needs to separate truth, framing, and action.

pages.title: Evidence Types
pages.summary: Studies, filings, datasets, regulator notices, named experts, leaks, and anonymous posts carry different kinds of reliability.

pages.title: Community Notes
pages.summary: Community Notes can add context to misleading posts, but their trust, speed, coverage and stability are different questions.

pages.title: Data Voids
pages.summary: When reliable results are scarce, the first confident-looking claim can dominate before better evidence appears.

pages.title: Eyewitness Posts
pages.summary: Eyewitness clips can reveal real events early, but time, place, angle and reposting can all change what they seem to show.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Evidence Types.

pages.title: Official Records
pages.summary: Corporate and legal claims need primary records because screenshots can hide context, amendments and what a filing actually proves.

pages.title: Regulator Notices
pages.summary: Regulator warnings are strong evidence of official concern, but they rarely settle every fact or future outcome on their own.

pages.title: Viral Charts
pages.summary: A chart can make a pattern look settled, but the dataset, sampling and methods decide whether the pattern is real.

pages.title: Health Claims
pages.summary: Health claims can feel urgent and personal, so they need careful checks of evidence type, source incentives, and medical context.

pages.title: Accuracy Checks
pages.summary: A brief accuracy check can interrupt the impulse to share dramatic health claims before checking their evidence.

pages.title: AI Doctor Deepfakes
pages.summary: AI doctor deepfakes exploit visual trust by making weak or fabricated claims look medically endorsed.

pages.title: Cancer Claims
pages.summary: Cancer cure claims become most dangerous when they persuade patients to replace proven treatment with untested products.

pages.title: Hidden Cures
pages.summary: Hidden-cure posts often turn weak clues into urgent treatment advice before human evidence can support the leap.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Health Claims.

pages.title: Natural Risks
pages.summary: Natural supplements can still be active drugs in practice, especially when they interact with prescriptions.

pages.title: Corroboration
pages.summary: Urgent claims about disasters, politics, war, health, or crime should be checked against independent sources before sharing.

pages.title: Source Trail
pages.summary: The strongest check is often not another share, but finding who first made the claim and what evidence they actually had.

pages.title: False Echoes
pages.summary: Many matching posts can still be one weak claim repeated through screenshots, reposts, summaries, and influencer retellings.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Corroboration.

pages.title: Crisis Rules
pages.summary: Platform crisis rules aim to slow harmful rumours when normal moderation is too slow for fast-moving public emergencies.

pages.title: Safety Claims
pages.summary: For crime and emergency posts, useful confirmation usually comes from sources close to the event and accountable for corrections.

pages.title: Southport Case
pages.summary: False claims after the Southport killings showed how misidentified suspects can move from online rumour to public disorder.

pages.title: Risk Triggers
pages.summary: Some posts need more checking because they ask people to blame, panic, donate, buy, avoid a place, or share immediately.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Critical thinking in the age of social media and A.

pages.title: Influencers
pages.summary: People often judge claims through social identity and familiar messengers, which can blur the line between trust and evidence.

pages.title: AI Impersonation
pages.summary: AI tools can imitate polish, intimacy and local detail, making fabricated messengers or claims look more credible.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Influencers.

pages.title: Social Proof
pages.summary: Visible approval signals can make weak or misleading posts look more reliable before readers check the evidence.

pages.title: Local Groups
pages.summary: In places with weaker local journalism, familiar community voices can become trusted shortcuts for rumours and public claims.

pages.title: News Influencers
pages.summary: News influencers can make current affairs feel more accessible while shifting trust from editorial process to personality.

pages.title: Parasocial Trust
pages.summary: Familiar creators can make public claims feel like advice from someone the audience already knows and likes.

pages.title: Shared Identity
pages.summary: A claim can feel safer than it is when it comes from someone who seems to understand your group or experience.

pages.title: Lateral Reading
pages.summary: Good online verification often starts by leaving the page and checking what independent sources say about the claim.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Lateral Reading.

pages.title: Surface Trust
pages.summary: Professional design, dot-org domains and confident biographies can create trust before the source has earned it.

pages.title: Real Source
pages.summary: A viral post is often only the last stop in a longer source trail, and finding the origin can change how much trust it deserves.

pages.title: SIFT Routine
pages.summary: SIFT gives readers a simple sequence for pausing, checking the source, finding better coverage and tracing evidence.

pages.title: Sponsored Content
pages.summary: Native advertising can blur the boundary between news and promotion unless readers check labels and source context.

pages.title: Fact Checker Study
pages.summary: Professional fact-checkers often judged unfamiliar websites faster because they left the page sooner.

pages.title: Video Checks
pages.summary: A video can be real but still mislead if it is old, clipped, or filmed somewhere else.

pages.title: Missing Context
pages.summary: A claim can be technically true but misleading when it hides timing, location, definitions, baselines, or comparison groups.

pages.title: AI Caveats
pages.summary: AI-written explanations can sound fluent while losing the dates, limitations, and uncertainty that keep a claim honest.

pages.title: Baselines
pages.summary: Words like 'surge', 'record', and 'highest since' only make sense when the starting point is visible.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Missing Context.

pages.title: Inner City
pages.summary: The '95%' inner-city claim shows how county baselines and undefined terms can reshape a public-safety statistic.

pages.title: Old Footage
pages.summary: Real footage can mislead when a new caption strips away the original date, place, and event.

pages.title: Pension Claim
pages.summary: The viral pension-pot claim shows how a wrong definition can make a calculation feel morally obvious but factually wrong.

pages.title: Denominators
pages.summary: A percentage can sound precise while hiding the population, period, or baseline that makes it meaningful.

pages.title: Mixed Feeds
pages.summary: When journalism, entertainment, activism, advertising, and synthetic content appear together, readers need stronger sorting habits.

pages.title: Influencers
pages.summary: Many people get news from influencers because it appears in entertainment spaces, not because they deliberately chose that source.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Mixed Feeds.

pages.title: News or opinion
pages.summary: A feed post may look news-like, but its trust value changes depending on whether it reports facts, argues a view, or reacts to someone else.

pages.title: Platform cues
pages.summary: Verification badges, view counts, avatars and polished video formats can feel like trust signals even when they only show visibility.

pages.title: Source memory
pages.summary: When stories arrive through search or social feeds, readers often lose the source cues that help them decide what to trust.

pages.title: Sponsored posts
pages.summary: Advertising inside ordinary posts can make persuasion look like recommendation, evidence or personal experience.

pages.title: Synthetic media
pages.summary: AI images and other synthetic posts make fast feed judgments harder because realism, humour and persuasion can arrive together.

pages.title: News Deserts
pages.summary: Local groups can become fertile ground for false authority messages when reliable local journalism is weak or absent.

pages.title: Council Checks
pages.summary: A viral claim about a council decision is easier to test when readers know which records, meetings and named officials to check.

pages.title: Fake Authority
pages.summary: False credibility often comes from borrowed institutional language, old images, manipulated screenshots or accounts that sound official.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on News Deserts.

pages.title: Election Rumors
pages.summary: Local elections sharpen misinformation because claims about candidates, services and identity can spread before reporters or officials respond.

pages.title: Local Groups
pages.summary: Neighborhood posts can feel trustworthy because they name familiar places, people and problems, even when the evidence is weak.

pages.title: Search Gaps
pages.summary: Searching is useful but often weak for local claims because the record may be thin, duplicated or dominated by the original rumor.

pages.title: SMF Dataset
pages.summary: The SMF analysis shows why news-related posts in local feeds can be much riskier than overall group activity suggests.

pages.title: Own Research
pages.summary: Responsible research means using a method for weighing evidence, not collecting links that confirm a preferred conclusion.

pages.title: AI Citations
pages.summary: AI can organize research, but fluent answers and realistic citations still need to be checked against original sources.

pages.title: Data Voids
pages.summary: Obscure phrases and breaking claims can create empty search spaces where low-quality sources look more important than they are.

pages.title: Search Backfire
pages.summary: Searching to check a false claim can backfire when weak results surround the reader with repetition instead of verification.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Own Research.

pages.title: Lateral Reading
pages.summary: Leaving the page to check who is behind it often reveals more than reading the page itself.

pages.title: Loaded Search
pages.summary: The words used to search a claim can quietly steer the results before any evidence is weighed.

pages.title: Opposing Evidence
pages.summary: A claim becomes stronger when it survives the best counterevidence, not when a reader only finds supporting links.

pages.title: Platform Incentives
pages.summary: Likes, comments, stitches, reposts, and algorithmic boosts can make performance feel more rewarding than accuracy.

pages.title: Accuracy Prompts
pages.summary: A small reminder to think about accuracy can make people more selective about what they repost next.

pages.title: Late Corrections
pages.summary: Corrective notes may reduce engagement once attached, but their impact depends heavily on whether they arrive before a post peaks.

pages.title: Outrage Ranking
pages.summary: Engagement-based feeds can turn anger, disbelief and correction into signals that push posts to more people.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Platform Incentives.

pages.title: Like Counts
pages.summary: Visible popularity signals can make a claim feel socially validated before anyone has checked the evidence behind it.

pages.title: Fast Formats
pages.summary: Low-friction formats can detach claims from sources, dates and missing context while making reposting feel effortless.

pages.title: Truth Rewards
pages.summary: Changing social rewards so they favour true information can improve discernment without assuming users are indifferent to truth.

pages.title: Primary Sources
pages.summary: Primary documents, regulator notices, court filings, and datasets can clarify what a viral interpretation leaves out.

pages.title: Robocall Trail
pages.summary: The New Hampshire AI robocall case shows why official records matter for who did what, when and under which law.

pages.title: Archived Pages
pages.summary: Archived pages can show what a source said before edits, deletions or quiet wording changes reshaped the claim.

pages.title: Court Records
pages.summary: A filing can prove that an argument was made, but only the court record shows whether a judge accepted it.

pages.title: Public Numbers
pages.summary: A public number is harder to trust when the table, date, definition or method behind it is missing.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Primary Sources.

pages.title: Regulator Status
pages.summary: Many viral posts collapse warnings, proposals, settlements and final orders into one misleading word: banned.

pages.title: VAERS Claims
pages.summary: VAERS can help detect possible safety signals, but raw reports cannot prove that a vaccine caused an event.

pages.title: Screenshots
pages.summary: Screenshots and reposted claims often hide the original source, date, edit history, and context needed to judge them.

pages.title: Late Notes
pages.summary: Corrections can reduce misinformation on live posts, but screenshots may keep the earlier false version moving elsewhere.

pages.title: Fake Posts
pages.summary: A convincing screenshot can name a real person or institution while showing words they never published.

pages.title: Fake Authority
pages.summary: Screenshots can borrow institutional authority by making false claims look like official statements during fast-moving events.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Screenshots.

pages.title: Local Groups
pages.summary: Neighbourhood reposts can make weak evidence feel stronger because the messenger is familiar and the claim feels close to home.

pages.title: Old Images
pages.summary: A real image can still mislead when a new caption detaches it from its original time, place or cause.

pages.title: Lost Satire
pages.summary: A joke or fake-post account can become misinformation when a repost strips away the cues that marked it as satire.

pages.title: Source Tracing
pages.summary: A useful AI answer is only as strong as the sources, data, and context a reader can trace behind it.

pages.title: News checks
pages.summary: AI news summaries can sound current while misidentifying sources, missing dates, or repeating outdated information.

pages.title: Citation checks
pages.summary: A citation only helps when the reader can open it, identify it, and confirm that it is not invented or dead.

pages.title: Link overload
pages.summary: Long link lists can create a false sense of certainty when the right sources are not matched to the right claims.

pages.title: Academic References
pages.summary: Fabricated papers and bibliographic details can make AI summaries look scholarly while hiding an unverifiable evidence trail.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Source Tracing.

pages.title: Court cases
pages.summary: Court filings show why fake AI citations are not harmless formatting errors when professional duties depend on verification.

pages.title: Wrong support
pages.summary: A working link can still mislead when it supports the general subject but not the specific sentence beside it.

pages.title: Synthetic Images
pages.summary: Realistic AI images make visual plausibility a weaker shortcut for deciding whether an event, quote, or document is genuine.

pages.title: Source Chain
pages.summary: The strongest question is not whether an image looks real, but what source trail connects it to a real place, time and witness.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Synthetic Images.

pages.title: Pentagon Fake
pages.summary: The fake Pentagon explosion showed how a synthetic image can matter during the short window before corroboration catches up.

pages.title: Pope Puffer
pages.summary: The Pope puffer image showed that low-stakes, funny fakes can still train people to trust style over source.

pages.title: Realism Trap
pages.summary: Photorealistic AI images can make false claims feel verified before viewers ask where the image came from.

pages.title: Reverse Search
pages.summary: Reverse image search can expose recycled photos, but newly generated images may leave no earlier copy to find.

pages.title: Inspection Limits
pages.summary: Hands, shadows and text can still reveal problems, but their absence no longer makes an image trustworthy.
